title: Vision
text: 한국어 English White & NRL Black & Yellow Search the website   SNU Robotics Institute Seoul National University  About › Vision  Vision   At a Glance Director’s Message Vision History Directions  A robotics ecosystem connecting education, research and entrepreneurship SNU Robotics Institute aims to bring together research expertise across disciplines and build an ecosystem in which the outcomes of education and research lead to practical technology applications and new ventures. Through this approach, we seek to become an internationally competitive research institute and to contribute to strengthening the competitiveness of Korea’s robotics industry. Creative technologies through interdisciplinary research We foster a research environment in which researchers from different fields define and solve problems together. By combining knowledge and research methods across departments and disciplines, we develop robotics technologies that would be difficult to achieve within a single field. Technology innovation driven by societal needs We pursue technologies that address real needs in society and industry. The requirements of users and application environments inform research planning, and the usefulness of new technologies is validated in the field. This process helps research outcomes translate into practical applications. Developing talent through hands-on education We establish an educational foundation that enables students to design, build and run experiments themselves. Research equipment, spaces and expertise are connected with education to give students experience in solving real problems. In this way, we develop robotics talent with both theoretical knowledge and practical implementation skills. Support from technology development to commercialization and entrepreneurship We are building a Lab to Market framework that provides continuous support for the technology development, scale-up and commercialization of research outcomes. Technical staff help advance technologies toward commercial use, while market experts and entrepreneurs identify application markets and business opportunities. Our aim is to connect the development of research technologies with preparations for launching new ventures. A research environment where researchers can keep taking on new challenges We envision a “Return to RI” support framework that enables researchers to return to the Institute after pursuing entrepreneurship and continue with further research and new initiatives. We aim to reduce the risks of entrepreneurship and bring experience gained in the field back into research and education.

title: Our Approach
description: Our Approach
text: Our Approach We know how to educate talent in the age of AI We live in an age when artificial intelligence answers our questions and summarizes knowledge for us. Information has never been easier to obtain, and for that very reason, what it means to truly know something is changing. SNU Robotics Institute believes that in the age of AI, the knowledge that remains one’s own comes from what one has confronted and worked through firsthand. That is why our education does not stop at making something by hand. Students define a problem, design their own robots, and then put those robots in a real arena to compete against robots built by their classmates. A design that looked perfect on paper falters in the face of friction, error and the unexpected, and in closing that gap, students learn how to turn an idea into technology that actually works. None of this is accomplished alone. Students divide roles, reconcile opinions and, at times, weather failure together. Learning from rivals and joining forces with teammates to push past their limits gives them something no lecture can replace: the firmest foundation for becoming an engineer. Design Define the problem and design and build a robot with your own hands. Compete in reality Test the finished robot on a real arena against other teams’ robots. Complete it together Work with teammates, learn from competitors and see it through. Imagine, design, collaborate and make it real. This is the educational philosophy of SNU Robotics Institute. Education like this demands a great deal of time, space and equipment, and the dedication of faculty and teaching assistants. It is by no means an easy path, but to uphold this philosophy we provide our students with hands-on education. It is this conviction that has kept Creative Engineering Design going for more than 30 years since it began in 1993. Imagine Design Collaborate Make it real

title: Creative Engineering Design
text: 한국어 English White & NRL Black & Yellow Search the website   SNU Robotics Institute Seoul National University  Education › Creative Engineering Design  Education   Creative Engineering Design Creative Engineering Design Program details and schedules will be announced here.  Developing talent through hands-on education SNU Robotics Institute pursues hands-on education in which students design, build and test robots themselves. We connect research equipment, spaces and the expertise of our researchers to teaching, so that students gain experience solving real problems. Through Creative Engineering Design and the Robotics Talent Program, we develop robotics talent with both theoretical understanding and the ability to build, and we aim for an ecosystem in which the outcomes of education carry through to research and entrepreneurship.   Creative Engineering Design  Creative Engineering Design is a project-based course in which first-year students in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Seoul National University work in teams to design and build their own robots. First introduced in 1993 by the late Professor Chong Nam Chu, it has continued for more than 30 years and has become a signature engineering course at the SNU College of Engineering.   About the Course  Students conceive robots that carry out a given mission, then build and test them within limited conditions to solve the problem. Along the way, they develop creativity, teamwork and engineering problem-solving skills. The course content has changed steadily to reflect advances in technology, and since 2024 it has used remote-control devices as a foundation for teaching AI robot architecture.    Curriculum    Machine Learning for Mechanical Engineering  Computer-aided design and software fundamentals    Creative Engineering Design  Robot hardware, motor control, basic circuits and building a working robot      SNU Robocon  The course culminates in Robocon, a team competition in which every student competes with the robot they built in class.    1993  First Creative Engineering Design robot competition    2022  30th anniversary of Creative Engineering Design and the 30th Robocon (Haedong Idea Factory). Winner: Team Zero; runner-up: Team Emergency Rescue; Engineering Award: Team-3; Creativity Award: Team Triple S    2024  The 32nd Robocon, held at the Haedong Advanced Engineering Building as Part 2 of SNU Robotics Day, with 60 students taking part. The winning team, “Jorip-wang” (Assembly King), earned a place in an international Robocon competition.      Student Voices    “Whenever we had an idea, we tested it, and we built our final robot from the ones that worked. When we won, I thought of everything we had been through and couldn’t hold back my tears.”  Team Zero, winner of the 30th Robocon    “Real-world variables cost us the title, but even if we could turn back time, we couldn’t have done better. We gave it everything.”  Team Emergency Rescue, runner-up of the 30th Robocon    “Determined to win the Robocon game, we stuck together all semester and lived with the rulebook. Because we were always thinking about winning, we had more ideas than we could use.”  Team-3, semifinalist of the 30th Robocon      This course aims to develop a sense of design and creativity by having students design and fabricate various objects through hands-on practice with Internet of Things (IoT) technology, which is widely used across industrial devices and home appliances including automobiles, robots, and smartphones. Building on this foundation, the course further extends to the implementation of Physical AI—artificial intelligence that perceives, reasons about, and acts upon the real world on its own. By utilizing microcontrollers (Arduino, 32-bit MCUs, etc.), students understand the basic structure of an MCU, collect data through various sensors such as temperature, humidity, light, sound, motion, and image, and learn the principles of connecting and controlling output devices such as displays and motors. On this basis, students connect objects through wired and wireless communication and implement on-device AI (TinyML), which learns from the collected data and runs inference directly on the device, thereby completing the entire process—from sensing to reasoning and action—as a single integrated system. The course is structured so that students with little experience in coding or hardware can learn step by step from the introductory stage, and by combining theory with hands-on practice, it connects with other engineering design courses, from the fundamentals through to prototype development. This course aims to develop a basic sense of design and fabrication, as well as creativity, through hands-on practice in designing and building a variety of assigned objects. Intended for first-year students who have not yet formed a clear concept of engineering, it has students build products themselves from specified materials and compete with them, so that they can experience the meaning of engineering with genuine interest. The products take many forms, such as mechanisms and structures, that together reflect the characteristics of various engineering fields. During the first six weeks, lectures on basic design principles, kinematics and fabrication methods are combined with robot programming practice and fabrication. The course consists of two hours of lecture and two hours of lab each week. In week 7, the purpose and rules of the robots that students will design and build are announced, and in week 12 the main competition is held with the robots each team has freely designed and built within the given rules, using the materials and tools provided.   Student Reviews  Reflections from teams that took part in the 30th Robocon (2022).     Team Zero  Winner   More classmates bet on Team Zero to win than on any other team.   Our TA told us later, “What you did is the textbook approach, but in practice people rarely do it.” When you just talk, there are plenty of good ideas. But until you build them, you can’t know whether they work. Whenever we had an idea, we built a simple version and tested it, and we built our final robot only from the ideas that proved to work. We thought every team did that, but it turned out they didn’t. When we won, I thought of everything we had been through and couldn’t hold back my tears.      Team Emergency Rescue  Runner-up   They swept into the final and were called “the best strategists,” but lost in the final.   With a week left, we tore down both of our robots, even though they had been rated well, and started over. Our TA asked if we were crazy, but we were determined to finish first, so we chose a week of all-nighters. In the evaluation rounds you only need to perform well on your own, but at Robocon robots face off against each other, so we thought we had to rebuild ours into a robot that could win. The strategy worked. Real-world variables cost us the title, but even if we could turn back time, we couldn’t have done better. We gave it everything.      Team-3  Semifinalist · Engineering Award   While every other team had two pilots, Team-3 was the only one flying solo, and it won the Engineering Award.   Determined to win the Robocon game, we stuck together all semester and lived with the rulebook. Because we were always thinking about winning, we had more ideas than we could use. We built and tested many versions over and over, and made it to the semifinals. I came to this department out of respect for mechanical engineering, which built aircraft carriers and went to the moon before the internet existed. After Robocon, though, I realized how important management and strategy are, so I’ve applied for a double major in a related field.      Team Triple S (SS.S)  Semifinalist · Creativity Award   They were eliminated in the semifinals, but their uniquely designed wheels earned the Creativity Award from a special jury.   I spent a lot of time on Creative Engineering Design. But spending a lot of time doesn’t mean things go as planned. Coming up with ideas, building all night, failing… meeting, rebuilding… and it was so much fun! I think I’d tell incoming students to take the course in their first year. It’s a shortcut to discovering your identity as a mechanical engineer, and if you’ve chosen the wrong department, you’ll find that out through the course too.      Team MEshiah  Quarterfinalist   They built a robot that was excellent in physical terms but, by their own account, lost in the quarterfinals because no one was thinking about a strategy to win.   When we formed the team, we thought the title was ours. We all went to the same high school, and though our dreams differ, we came together because we all love physics. We believed we had built the best robot in physical terms, and our first and second evaluation results were good. Not thinking much about how to beat the other robots is what stopped us in the quarterfinals. My dream is to become a CEO, and the course felt a lot like starting a company, so I learned a great deal.      Team ABCÉD  Round of 16   Strong title contenders, they narrowly lost in the round of 16.   When a preliminary match went wrong, we were offered a rematch, but we believed an unbreakable spirit mattered more, so we proudly chose to bow out. Our team is a group of true believers who love physics and math and love machines that move. No regrets. Right after withdrawing, we went straight to the gym to rebuild the stamina we had lost. TC 01 · MORPHI BODY Adaptive Robot Materials, Structures and Physical Intelligence Why it matters Robots that move in contact with people must respond safely to unpredictable changes. Handling every response through sensors and complex control algorithms increases computation and energy demand. This is why robots need materials and structures that themselves distribute forces and comply with their surroundings, going beyond the limits of a fixed body. Research approach MORPHI Body combines physical intelligence with variable structures that change shape and stiffness to suit the environment. Mechanisms are designed to find balance and distribute forces, allowing the body itself to perform part of the computation and control. We also study how robots sense their own physical state and respond to bodily changes, aiming for safe interaction and affordable, energy-efficient hardware. Real-world settings also require immediate responses to contact with people and changes in task conditions. Robots therefore need an architecture that can learn and reconfigure individual functions while coordinating overall behavior. Research approach Inspired by functional specialization and coordination in the brain, MOSAIC Intelligence studies an architecture in which a higher-level global intelligence coordinates local intelligence for each body part and function. Local modules learn physical interactions and movement, while global intelligence interprets situations and goals and coordinates their cooperation. We study module recomposition and continual learning across both levels to enable efficient adaptation to different bodies and tasks. Faster robot design, learning and validation require accurate, rapid simulation of complex interactions alongside consistent management of diverse data. Research approach The Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin connects multiphysics simulation, a data fabric and integrated software–hardware optimization. Robots that directly affect people’s bodies and daily lives must account for human values, including safety, functioning and autonomy. Rather than only evaluating ethics or usability after development is complete, a framework is needed that reflects and verifies these values from initial design through control and real-world validation. Research approach Human Value studies a Value Operating System (Value OS) that translates human-centered values into design decisions and control principles that can be verified throughout development. Scenarios reflecting clinical and social contexts are used to examine robot behavior and risks to human values, with findings fed back into subsequent designs. The aim is to lay a foundation for comparing and judging robots’ clinical reliability and social acceptance against consistent criteria. title: TC 1 · Adaptive Robot Materials, Structures and Physical Intelligence
text: TC 01 · MORPHI BODY Adaptive Robot Materials, Structures and Physical Intelligence Why it matters Robots that move in contact with people must respond safely to unpredictable changes. Handling every response through sensors and complex control algorithms increases computation and energy demand. This is why robots need materials and structures that themselves distribute forces and comply with their surroundings, going beyond the limits of a fixed body. Research approach MORPHI Body combines physical intelligence with variable structures that change shape and stiffness to suit the environment. Mechanisms are designed to find balance and distribute forces, allowing the body itself to perform part of the computation and control. We also study how robots sense their own physical state and respond to bodily changes, aiming for safe interaction and affordable, energy-efficient hardware. Key research topics Reconfigurable actuation and structures: joints with actively adjustable shape and stiffness, and bio-inspired artificial muscles Self-sensing skin: soft distributed tactile sensors and systems for monitoring the robot’s physical state Modularity and reliability: shared specifications and durability and reliability evaluation for low-cost, low-power hardware Leaders Cho, Kyu-Jin Leader Deputy leaders Han, Kyung Won Deputy leader View researchers 19 Participating Faculty 14 Kang, Ji Heong Dept. of Chemistry Ko, Seung Hwan Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Kim, Jinsoo Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Kim, Ho-young Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Park, Yong-lae Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Yang, Jinkyu Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Lee, Howon Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Jung, Gyuweon School of Transdisciplinary Innovations Cho, Kyu-Jin Leader Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Ha, Jung-ik Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Han, Kyung Won Deputy leader Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Han, Bohyung Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Hong, Yongtaek Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Sun, Jeong-yun Dept. of Materials Science and Engineering Affiliated Faculty 5 Kim, Taeyong Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Park, Seongjun School of Transdisciplinary Innovations Ahn, Sung-hoon Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Yu, Youngjae School of Transdisciplinary Innovations Yoon, Tae-young Dept. of Biological Sciences

title: TC 2 · Cooperative Distributed Intelligence and Continual Learning
text: TC 02 · MOSAIC INTELLIGENCE Cooperative Distributed Intelligence and Continual Learning Why it matters Retraining an entire intelligence system whenever a robot’s body or task environment changes demands substantial time and computing resources. Real-world settings also require immediate responses to contact with people and changes in task conditions. Robots therefore need an architecture that can learn and reconfigure individual functions while coordinating overall behavior. Research approach Inspired by functional specialization and coordination in the brain, MOSAIC Intelligence studies an architecture in which a higher-level global intelligence coordinates local intelligence for each body part and function. Local modules learn physical interactions and movement, while global intelligence interprets situations and goals and coordinates their cooperation. We study module recomposition and continual learning across both levels to enable efficient adaptation to different bodies and tasks. Key research topics Autonomous local intelligence: modules that perceive the physical properties of robots, humans and environments and learn movement independently Contextual global intelligence: understanding and predicting situations to coordinate perception and movement modules Continual learning and co-evolution: local and global intelligence learning together and adapting to new environments and missions Leaders Kwak, Nojun Leader Lee, Inah Leader View researchers 29 Participating Faculty 13 Ko, Seung Hwan Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Kwak, Nojun Leader Dept. of Intelligence & Information Kim, Young Min Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Kim, Ju Han College of Medicine Kim, Jinsoo Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Kim, Taesup Graduate School of Data Science Park, Frank C. title: TC 3 · Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin
text: TC 03 · ROBOT–HUMAN–ENVIRONMENT DIGITAL TWIN Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin Why it matters Predicting contact between people and robots in changing environments requires multiple physical phenomena to be considered together. Existing digital twins can be fragmented by phenomenon, or face a trade-off between prediction accuracy and computing speed. Faster robot design, learning and validation require accurate, rapid simulation of complex interactions alongside consistent management of diverse data. Research approach The Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin connects multiphysics simulation, a data fabric and integrated software–hardware optimization. We study how to generate and augment physically consistent data in virtual experiments and connect it with real-world observations for iterative robot design and validation. The aim is an integrated framework that supports everyday assistance, wearable and intra-body robots under their different operating conditions. Key research topics Digital twin: high-accuracy, high-speed simulation of complex physical interactions and generation of data for learning and validation Data fabric: generating, augmenting, storing and managing large-scale data in diverse formats while preserving physical consistency and context Infrastructure optimization: integrated software–hardware design for efficient simulation and data processing Leaders Kim, Donyun Leader Deputy leaders Jung, Hyungsoo Deputy leader View researchers 19 Participating Faculty 11 Kim, Donyun Leader Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Kim, Jinsoo Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Park, Moon Seok College of Medicine (Bundang) Park, Hyungmin Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Ahn, Jooeun Dept. of Physical Education Yang, Jinkyu Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Oh, Joo Hwan Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Won, Jungdam Dept. of Computer Science & Engineering Jung, Hyungsoo Deputy leader Graduate School of Data Science Han, Bohyung Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Lee, Jae W. title: TC 4 · Robot Safety, Clinical Reliability and Social Acceptance
text: TC 04 · HUMAN VALUE Robot Safety, Clinical Reliability and Social Acceptance Why it matters Higher performance alone does not make a robot beneficial or trustworthy. Robots that directly affect people’s bodies and daily lives must account for human values, including safety, functioning and autonomy. Rather than only evaluating ethics or usability after development is complete, a framework is needed that reflects and verifies these values from initial design through control and real-world validation. Research approach Human Value studies a Value Operating System (Value OS) that translates human-centered values into design decisions and control principles that can be verified throughout development. Scenarios reflecting clinical and social contexts are used to examine robot behavior and risks to human values, with findings fed back into subsequent designs. The aim is to lay a foundation for comparing and judging robots’ clinical reliability and social acceptance against consistent criteria. Key research topics Value-based design: defining indicators for safety, functioning and autonomy and using them in design and validation Demonstration and stress testing: identifying thresholds of value compromise across interaction scenarios and explaining the basis for each judgment Shared criteria and design feedback: studying a Human Value API and reliability criteria, and feeding evaluation results into control and design improvements Leaders Kim, Hongsoo Leader Deputy leaders Park, Hyunwoo Deputy leader View researchers 19 Participating Faculty 12 Kim, Kee Won College of Medicine Kim, Young Min Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Kim, Hyeoneui College of Nursing Kim, Hongsoo Leader Graduate School of Public Health Park, Juyeon Dept. of Textiles, Merchandising & Fashion Design Park, Hyunwoo Deputy leader Graduate School of Data Science Baek, Sung Hee Dept. of Biological Sciences Seo, Jongmo Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Yoon, Chang Hwan College of Medicine (Bundang) Lee, Joonhwan Dept. of Communication Jeong, Chang Wook College of Medicine Jo, Yohan Graduate School of Data Science Affiliated Faculty 7 Ro, Du Hyun College of Medicine Mook-Jung, Inhee College of Medicine Park, Myungwoo College of Medicine (Boramae) Park, Sangchul School of Law Beom, Jaewon College of Medicine (Bundang) Ahn, Woo-young Dept. of Psychology Lee, Soo-hyun Dept. of Psychology
